scenario.name: Microsoft Sysinternals & Splunk SURGe DFIR — LSASS MiniDump via comsvcs.dll & Sysmon EventID 10
scenario.shortSubtitle: Credential Access · rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll,#24, OpenProcess(0x1010) & MDMP Forensics
scenario.overview: Imagine an armored marble bank safe-deposit vault where every VIP safety-deposit box holds golden master passkeys behind a circular brushed-steel vault door, watched from across the hall by a glass security guard booth. Instead of bringing bolt cutters or breaking the hinges, a rogue insider flashes an elevated golden inspector badge, calls in the bank’s own certified brass-framed vault photographer carrying an official X-ray camera, and asks the photographer to snap a full cross-section X-ray photograph of every open safety-deposit drawer inside the vault. In a single bright crimson camera flash, an instant X-ray photo negative slides out onto a plain cardboard packing table in the hallway, where the insider drops it into an unlabeled courier envelope to develop the master passkeys offline later, never realizing the glass security guard booth logged the exact X-ray camera badge number, the camera’s wide-open lens setting, and the exact aisle path straight to the vault door. In this flagship Windows DFIR scenario (MITRE ATT&CK T1134, T1218.011, and T1003.001) grounded in Microsoft Sysinternals, Microsoft Learn, and Splunk SURGe research, an elevated administrator dumps LSASS credentials on WKS-ADM-07 using only built-in signed Microsoft binaries. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: verifying SeDebugPrivilege and lsass.exe PID 684, then invoking Microsoft-signed rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll MiniDump (or ordinal #24) to acquire a 0x1010 PROCESS_VM_READ handle, then writing a 48.2 MB MDMP snapshot (C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp) for offline NTLM/Kerberos extraction, while Sysmon Event ID 10 CallTrace correlation exposes the theft and RunAsPPL blocks it at the kernel layer. Steps #1-#4 trace every forensic artifact end-to-end, and Memory Forensics contrasts unprotected LSASS reads against RunAsPPL kernel enforcement.

stages.title: SeDebugPrivilege Elevation & LSASS Process ID (PID 684) Discovery
stages.subtitle: High-Integrity Admin Token Confirmed via EID 4672 Before Targeting lsass.exe
stages.description: At the administrative brass desk on the left side of the marble bank hall, a rogue insider flashes an elevated golden inspector badge that unlocks private back-office access. Before summoning the photographer, the insider checks the bank’s glowing room directory plaque to note the exact vault door number where the VIP safety-deposit boxes sit. Windows blocks standard users from reading another system process’s memory, so LSASS dumping first requires a High-integrity administrative token holding SeDebugPrivilege (a privileged right allowing a process to inspect and open handles to SYSTEM processes). Security Event ID 4672 records SeDebugPrivilege assignment at logon for CORP\adm_jchen, and the operator executes tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe" from cmd.exe (PID 4920) to resolve the live numeric Process ID (684) that comsvcs.dll expects as its first MiniDump parameter. Because comsvcs.dll!MiniDump requires a numeric target Process ID rather than a symbolic process name, attackers almost always enumerate lsass.exe via tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe", PowerShell Get-Process lsass, or wmic process get Name,ProcessId moments before executing rundll32.exe. Internally, Windows kernel SeSinglePrivilegeCheck honors SeDebugPrivilege (privilege LUID 20) to override standard discretionary access control lists on SYSTEM processes, making a High-integrity Security Event ID 4672 followed within seconds by lsass.exe PID discovery an early, high-signal precursor before any credential bytes ever leave memory. In the documented Security EID 4672 / Sysmon 1 exchange from cmd.exe (PID 4920) to rundll32.exe (PID 5412), rundll32.exe (PID 5412) responds with ACK PID 684 (confirming that the SEDEBUG + PID ENUM request succeeded on rundll32.exe (PID 5412) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Signed LOLBin Execution (rundll32.exe + comsvcs.dll,#24) & OpenProcess(0x1010)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SEDEBUG + PID ENUM / ⇠#1 ACK PID 684) from Node ① (#1 cmd.exe (PID 4920)) to Node ② (#2 rundll32.exe (PID 5412)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch).

stages.title: Signed LOLBin Execution (rundll32.exe + comsvcs.dll,#24) & OpenProcess(0x1010)
stages.subtitle: Microsoft-Signed DLL Requests PROCESS_VM_READ on lsass.exe (Sysmon EID 10)
stages.description: Instead of smuggling contraband tools past the front door, the insider wheels the bank’s own certified brass-framed vault photographer right down the marble aisle to the circular steel vault door. Turning the brass aperture ring wide open on the official X-ray camera, the photographer requests full read-through viewing access straight into the glowing vault drawers. To evade antivirus signatures targeting Mimikatz or ProcDump, the operator runs Microsoft-signed C:\Windows\System32\rundll32.exe (Windows’ native DLL execution proxy binary) pointing at C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 684 C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp full (or substitutes export ordinal #24 so naive command-line filters matching the literal word MiniDump miss the launch). Internally, comsvcs.dll enables SeDebugPrivilege via RtlAdjustPrivilege (the native Windows syscall that activates held privileges on the current token) and calls OpenProcess against lsass.exe (PID 684) with GrantedAccess 0x1010 (a minimal access mask combining PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION and PROCESS_VM_READ to read remote memory), triggering a high-fidelity Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess kernel callback record) whose CallTrace stack explicitly lists comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.dll. Because both rundll32.exe and comsvcs.dll are legitimately Microsoft-signed system binaries already residing in C:\Windows\System32, hash-based allowlists, AppLocker default publisher rules, and file-reputation filters will not block them, and switching from the export name "MiniDump" to ordinal "#24" (or copying comsvcs.dll to a renamed temp path) defeats naive command-line string rules. However, Windows kernel ObRegisterCallbacks inside Sysmon64.sys intercepts every NtOpenProcess call targeting lsass.exe, logging GrantedAccess 0x1010 and unwinding the user-mode stack CallTrace through comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.dll with near-zero false positives. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ OPENPROCESS 0x1010 / ⇠#2 ACK 0x1010) from Node ② (#2 rundll32.exe (PID 5412)) to Node ③ (#3 comsvcs.dll -> dbgcore.dll), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch).

stages.title: MiniDumpWriteDump Full-Memory Serialization to C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp
stages.subtitle: 48.2 MB MDMP (4D 44 4D 50 93 A7) Snapshot Captures NTLM & Kerberos RAM
stages.description: With the vault glass swung into cutaway view, the brass X-ray camera fires a blazing crimson flash directly through every VIP safety-deposit box inside the vault. Moments later, an instant X-ray photo negative slides out of the camera onto a corridor packing table and slips into a plain courier sleeve so the insider can study every master passkey quietly off-site. Once OpenProcess returns a valid handle to lsass.exe (PID 684), comsvcs.dll invokes dbgcore.dll!MiniDumpWriteDump using the MiniDumpWithFullMemory (0x2) flag. Windows reads the private virtual memory pages of lsasrv.dll!LogonSessionList (0x00007FF7A8100000), msv1_0.dll, and kerberos.dll (0x00007FFAD4200000), writing a 48.2 MB minidump file to C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp that begins with the unmistakable 6-byte signature 4D 44 4D 50 93 A7 ("MDMP") (When the operator passes the trailing "full" keyword to comsvcsdll!MiniDump, dbgcoredll sets MINIDUMP_TYPE = MiniDumpWithFullMemory 0x00000002, enumerating every readable virtual memory range in lsassexe via NtQueryVirtualMemory and copying them via NtReadVirtualMemory into the output file handle Renaming the output dump to look harmless such as reporttxt, cachedat, or logopng does not change its 6-byte magic header 4D 44 4D 50 93 A7 or its embedded ModuleListStream entries for lsasrvdll and msv1_0dll, so Sysmon Event ID 11 paired with YARA header inspection reliably unmasks the stolen memory snapshot). When the operator passes the trailing "full" keyword to comsvcs.dll!MiniDump, dbgcore.dll sets MINIDUMP_TYPE = MiniDumpWithFullMemory (0x00000002), enumerating every readable virtual memory range in lsass.exe via NtQueryVirtualMemory and copying them via NtReadVirtualMemory into the output file handle. Renaming the output dump to look harmless (such as report.txt, cache.dat, or logo.png) does not change its 6-byte magic header (4D 44 4D 50 93 A7) or its embedded ModuleListStream entries for lsasrv.dll and msv1_0.dll, so Sysmon Event ID 11 paired with YARA header inspection reliably unmasks the stolen memory snapshot. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ WRITE MDMP DUMP / ⇠#3 ACK 48.2 MB MDMP) from Node ③ (#3 comsvcs.dll -> dbgcore.dll) to Node ④ (#4 lsass.exe (PID 684)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch).

stages.title: Offline Credential Parsing (pypykatz) vs. Sysmon EID 10 & RunAsPPL Defense
stages.subtitle: Zero Mimikatz on Disk Caught by CallTrace Correlation & Blocked by PPL
stages.description: Even though the insider carries the sealed X-ray negative out of the building to develop the golden passkeys in a distant darkroom, the elevated glass security guard booth has already caught every movement on its central monitor. Locking a violet spotlight beam straight onto the photographer’s camera path, the chief guard triggers an immediate alert and slams an unbreakable steel blast shield across every bank vault so no X-ray lens can ever peer through again. After exfiltrating C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp off WKS-ADM-07, the attacker parses it offline with pypykatz (pypykatz lsa minidump debug.dmp) or Mimikatz to recover NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs without ever running cracking tools on the monitored endpoint. Defenders defeat this entire class of Living-off-the-Land credential theft in two layers: (1) correlating Sysmon Event ID 1 + Event ID 10 (CallTrace: comsvcs.dll + dbgcore.dll) + Event ID 11 in SIEM/EDR for instant containment, and (2) enabling kernel-enforced LSA Protection (RunAsPPL = 1) plus VBS-backed Windows Defender Credential Guard (LsaIso.exe) so rundll32.exe receives STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED (0xC0000022) before reading a single byte of lsass.exe. Because offline dumping decouples credential extraction from the compromised workstation, waiting for endpoint Mimikatz binary signatures is too late, even if the attacker deletes C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp immediately after exfiltration, centralized SIEM forwarding retains the ProcessGuid-linked triad of Sysmon EID 1, EID 10, and EID 11. Permanently closing this attack surface requires enabling HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL = 1 (PsProtectedSignerLsa-Light, which rejects non-PPL OpenProcess calls at PsTestProtectedProcessIncompatibility) alongside VBS Credential Guard (isolating NTLM/TGT secrets inside VTL1 LsaIso.exe) and Defender ASR LSASS blocking. On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ EID 10 + PPL AUDIT / ⇠#4 ALERT ALERT + PPL) from Node ④ (#4 lsass.exe (PID 684)) to Node ⑤ (#5 C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch).

detectionRule.title: Administrative Discovery of LSASS Process ID Preceding Credential Dumping
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: LSASS Process ID Enumeration via Command Line
status: stable
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\tasklist.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\wmic.exe'
  selection_lsass:
    CommandLine|contains: 'lsass'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_lsass
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.001
  - attack.t1134
detectionRule.mitigation: Remove SeDebugPrivilege from non-essential accounts, enforce Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and restrict local administrator membership via LAPS and Tier-0 separation.

detectionRule.title: LSASS ProcessAccess via comsvcs.dll MiniDump (Sysmon Event ID 10)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: LSASS Memory Access via comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.dll CallTrace
status: stable
logsource:
  category: process_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_target:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
  selection_access:
    GrantedAccess|endswith:
      - '1010'
      - '1410'
      - '1438'
      - '143a'
      - '1fffff'
  selection_trace:
    CallTrace|contains|all:
      - 'comsvcs.dll'
      - 'dbgcore.dll'

detectionRule.title: Windows LSASS Minidump (MDMP) File Containing lsasrv.dll & msv1_0.dll Streams
detectionRule.ruleCode:
rule DFIR_LSASS_MDMP_Minidump_Artifact {
  meta:
    description = "Detects renamed or staged Windows minidump files containing LSASS credential modules"
    mitre = "T1003.001"
  strings:
    $mdmp = { 4D 44 4D 50 93 A7 }
    $lsasrv = "lsasrv.dll" wide ascii
    $msv1 = "msv1_0.dll" wide ascii
    $kerb = "kerberos.dll" wide ascii
  condition:
    $mdmp at 0 and 2 of ($lsasrv, $msv1, $kerb)
}
detectionRule.mitigation: Deploy EDR file-inspection rules alerting on any MDMP magic header (4D 44 4D 50 93 A7) written by rundll32.exe into Temp or Public directories regardless of file extension (.dmp, .txt, .png).

detectionRule.title: Suspicious rundll32.exe Execution of comsvcs.dll MiniDump (Name or Ordinal #24)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Comsvcs.dll MiniDump Execution via Rundll32 (Name or Ordinal #24)
status: stable
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    Image|endswith: '\rundll32.exe'
  selection_dll:
    CommandLine|contains: 'comsvcs'
  selection_export:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'MiniDump'
      - '#24'
      - '#00024'
      - 'full'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_dll and selection_export
level: high
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.001
  - attack.t1218.011
detectionRule.mitigation: Enforce Microsoft Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rule "Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)", enable RunAsPPL + Credential Guard via GPO/Intune, and rotate any exposed NTLM/Kerberos credentials immediately.

briefing.headline: Scenario Briefing: LSASS MiniDump via comsvcs.dll & Sysmon EventID 10 (T1003.001)
briefing.storyAnalogy: Imagine an armored marble bank safe-deposit vault where every VIP safety-deposit box holds golden master passkeys behind a circular brushed-steel vault door, watched from across the hall by a glass security guard booth. Instead of bringing bolt cutters or breaking the hinges, a rogue insider flashes an elevated golden inspector badge, calls in the bank’s own certified brass-framed vault photographer carrying an official X-ray camera, and asks the photographer to snap a full cross-section X-ray photograph of every open safety-deposit drawer inside the vault. In a single bright crimson camera flash, an instant X-ray photo negative slides out onto a plain cardboard packing table in the hallway, where the insider drops it into an unlabeled courier envelope to develop the master passkeys offline later, never realizing the glass security guard booth logged the exact X-ray camera badge number, the camera’s wide-open lens setting, and the exact aisle path straight to the vault door.

storyMappings.technicalTerm: lsass.exe (PID 684) Hosting MSV1_0 NTLM & Kerberos Credentials

storyMappings.storyTerm: Instant X-Ray Negative on Packing Table

briefing.plainSummary: In this flagship Windows DFIR scenario (MITRE ATT&CK T1134, T1218.011, and T1003.001) grounded in Microsoft Sysinternals, Microsoft Learn, and Splunk SURGe research, an elevated administrator dumps LSASS credentials on WKS-ADM-07 using only built-in signed Microsoft binaries. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: verifying SeDebugPrivilege and lsass.exe PID 684, then invoking Microsoft-signed rundll32.exe with comsvcs.dll MiniDump (or ordinal #24) to acquire a 0x1010 PROCESS_VM_READ handle, then writing a 48.2 MB MDMP snapshot (C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp) for offline NTLM/Kerberos extraction, while Sysmon Event ID 10 CallTrace correlation exposes the theft and RunAsPPL blocks it at the kernel layer. Steps #1-#4 trace every forensic artifact end-to-end, and Memory Forensics contrasts unprotected LSASS reads against RunAsPPL kernel enforcement.
briefing.diagramTopologySummary: On the diagram: Follow Step #1 from Node ① (cmd.exe PID 4920 with SeDebugPrivilege) resolving PID 684, watch Step #2 spawn Node ② (rundll32.exe PID 5412) and invoke Node ③ (comsvcs.dll -> dbgcore.dll) to open Node ④ (lsass.exe PID 684), see Step #3 write Node ⑤ (C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp 48.2 MB MDMP), and track Step #4 as Node ⑥ (Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch) exposes the CallTrace and enforces RunAsPPL.
briefing.documentedAdvisory: Microsoft Sysinternals Sysmon EID 10 · Microsoft Learn RunAsPPL & MiniDumpWriteDump · Splunk SURGe & LOLBAS comsvcs.dll

steps.storyAnalogy: At the administrative brass desk on the left side of the marble bank hall, a rogue insider flashes an elevated golden inspector badge that unlocks private back-office access. Before summoning the photographer, the insider checks the bank’s glowing room directory plaque to note the exact vault door number where the VIP safety-deposit boxes sit.
steps.simpleExplanation: Windows blocks standard users from reading another system process’s memory, so LSASS dumping first requires a High-integrity administrative token holding SeDebugPrivilege (a privileged right allowing a process to inspect and open handles to SYSTEM processes). Security Event ID 4672 records SeDebugPrivilege assignment at logon for CORP\adm_jchen, and the operator executes tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe" from cmd.exe (PID 4920) to resolve the live numeric Process ID (684) that comsvcs.dll expects as its first MiniDump parameter.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Because comsvcs.dll!MiniDump requires a numeric target Process ID rather than a symbolic process name, attackers almost always enumerate lsass.exe via tasklist /fi "imagename eq lsass.exe", PowerShell Get-Process lsass, or wmic process get Name,ProcessId moments before executing rundll32.exe. Internally, Windows kernel SeSinglePrivilegeCheck honors SeDebugPrivilege (privilege LUID 20) to override standard discretionary access control lists on SYSTEM processes, making a High-integrity Security Event ID 4672 followed within seconds by lsass.exe PID discovery an early, high-signal precursor before any credential bytes ever leave memory.
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, Step #1 starts at Node ① (cmd.exe PID 4920 on WKS-ADM-07) confirming SeDebugPrivilege and staging Node ② (rundll32.exe PID 5412), observed by Node ⑥ (Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch).
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Correlate Windows Security Event ID 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned containing SeDebugPrivilege) with Sysmon Event ID 1 / Windows Security Event ID 4688 process creation logs showing cmd.exe (PID 4920) or PowerShell querying lsass.exe process IDs, enforced via Sigma hunting rules in SIEM and EDR telemetry.

storyMappings.technicalTerm: SeDebugPrivilege Assigned at Logon (Security Event ID 4672)
Mandatory Numeric Target PID Argument Required by comsvcs.dll

steps.plainTitle: Signed rundll32.exe Proxy & comsvcs.dll Ordinal #24 OpenProcess(0x1010)
steps.storyAnalogy: Instead of smuggling contraband tools past the front door, the insider wheels the bank’s own certified brass-framed vault photographer right down the marble aisle to the circular steel vault door. Turning the brass aperture ring wide open on the official X-ray camera, the photographer requests full read-through viewing access straight into the glowing vault drawers.
steps.simpleExplanation: To evade antivirus signatures targeting Mimikatz or ProcDump, the operator runs Microsoft-signed C:\Windows\System32\rundll32.exe (Windows’ native DLL execution proxy binary) pointing at C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 684 C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp full (or substitutes export ordinal #24 so naive command-line filters matching the literal word MiniDump miss the launch). Internally, comsvcs.dll enables SeDebugPrivilege via RtlAdjustPrivilege (the native Windows syscall that activates held privileges on the current token) and calls OpenProcess against lsass.exe (PID 684) with GrantedAccess 0x1010 (a minimal access mask combining PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION and PROCESS_VM_READ to read remote memory), triggering a high-fidelity Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess kernel callback record) whose CallTrace stack explicitly lists comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.dll.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Because both rundll32.exe and comsvcs.dll are legitimately Microsoft-signed system binaries already residing in C:\Windows\System32, hash-based allowlists, AppLocker default publisher rules, and file-reputation filters will not block them, and switching from the export name "MiniDump" to ordinal "#24" (or copying comsvcs.dll to a renamed temp path) defeats naive command-line string rules. However, Windows kernel ObRegisterCallbacks inside Sysmon64.sys intercepts every NtOpenProcess call targeting lsass.exe, logging GrantedAccess 0x1010 and unwinding the user-mode stack CallTrace through comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.dll with near-zero false positives.
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, Step #2 flows from Node ② (rundll32.exe PID 5412) through Node ③ (comsvcs.dll -> dbgcore.dll) into Node ④ (lsass.exe PID 684) while Node ⑥ (Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch) logs GrantedAccess=0x1010 and CallTrace.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Inspect Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) and EDR kernel handle telemetry for TargetImage ending in \lsass.exe with GrantedAccess masks 0x1010, 0x1410, or 0x1FFFFF where CallTrace includes comsvcs.dll and dbgcore.dll, paired with Sigma rules on Sysmon Event ID 1 catching rundll32.exe loading comsvcs.dll by name or ordinal #24.

storyMappings.technicalTerm: Export Ordinal #24 Evasion Bypassing "MiniDump" String Filters
lsass.exe (PID 684) Private RAM Holding Active Credential Sessions

steps.storyAnalogy: With the vault glass swung into cutaway view, the brass X-ray camera fires a blazing crimson flash directly through every VIP safety-deposit box inside the vault. Moments later, an instant X-ray photo negative slides out of the camera onto a corridor packing table and slips into a plain courier sleeve so the insider can study every master passkey quietly off-site.
steps.simpleExplanation: Once OpenProcess returns a valid handle to lsass.exe (PID 684), comsvcs.dll invokes dbgcore.dll!MiniDumpWriteDump using the MiniDumpWithFullMemory (0x2) flag. Windows reads the private virtual memory pages of lsasrv.dll!LogonSessionList (0x00007FF7A8100000), msv1_0.dll, and kerberos.dll (0x00007FFAD4200000), writing a 48.2 MB minidump file to C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp that begins with the unmistakable 6-byte signature 4D 44 4D 50 93 A7 ("MDMP") (When the operator passes the trailing "full" keyword to comsvcsdll!MiniDump, dbgcoredll sets MINIDUMP_TYPE = MiniDumpWithFullMemory 0x00000002, enumerating every readable virtual memory range in lsassexe via NtQueryVirtualMemory and copying them via NtReadVirtualMemory into the output file handle Renaming the output dump to look harmless such as reporttxt, cachedat, or logopng does not change its 6-byte magic header 4D 44 4D 50 93 A7 or its embedded ModuleListStream entries for lsasrvdll and msv1_0dll, so Sysmon Event ID 11 paired with YARA header inspection reliably unmasks the stolen memory snapshot).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: When the operator passes the trailing "full" keyword to comsvcs.dll!MiniDump, dbgcore.dll sets MINIDUMP_TYPE = MiniDumpWithFullMemory (0x00000002), enumerating every readable virtual memory range in lsass.exe via NtQueryVirtualMemory and copying them via NtReadVirtualMemory into the output file handle. Renaming the output dump to look harmless (such as report.txt, cache.dat, or logo.png) does not change its 6-byte magic header (4D 44 4D 50 93 A7) or its embedded ModuleListStream entries for lsasrv.dll and msv1_0.dll, so Sysmon Event ID 11 paired with YARA header inspection reliably unmasks the stolen memory snapshot.
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, Step #3 streams credential RAM from Node ④ (lsass.exe PID 684) via Node ③ (comsvcs.dll -> dbgcore.dll) onto Node ⑤ (C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp 48.2 MB MDMP), firing Sysmon Event ID 11 at Node ⑥ (Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch).
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Monitor Sysmon Event ID 11 (FileCreate) and EDR file telemetry for rundll32.exe (PID 5412) writing large multi-megabyte files into C:\Windows\Temp or C:\Users\Public, and run YARA memory/disk scans matching magic header 4D 44 4D 50 93 A7 alongside embedded lsasrv.dll and msv1_0.dll strings.

steps.plainTitle: Offline pypykatz Extraction vs. Sysmon CallTrace Hunting & RunAsPPL
steps.storyAnalogy: Even though the insider carries the sealed X-ray negative out of the building to develop the golden passkeys in a distant darkroom, the elevated glass security guard booth has already caught every movement on its central monitor. Locking a violet spotlight beam straight onto the photographer’s camera path, the chief guard triggers an immediate alert and slams an unbreakable steel blast shield across every bank vault so no X-ray lens can ever peer through again.
steps.simpleExplanation: After exfiltrating C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp off WKS-ADM-07, the attacker parses it offline with pypykatz (pypykatz lsa minidump debug.dmp) or Mimikatz to recover NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs without ever running cracking tools on the monitored endpoint. Defenders defeat this entire class of Living-off-the-Land credential theft in two layers: (1) correlating Sysmon Event ID 1 + Event ID 10 (CallTrace: comsvcs.dll + dbgcore.dll) + Event ID 11 in SIEM/EDR for instant containment, and (2) enabling kernel-enforced LSA Protection (RunAsPPL = 1) plus VBS-backed Windows Defender Credential Guard (LsaIso.exe) so rundll32.exe receives STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED (0xC0000022) before reading a single byte of lsass.exe.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Because offline dumping decouples credential extraction from the compromised workstation, waiting for endpoint Mimikatz binary signatures is too late, even if the attacker deletes C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp immediately after exfiltration, centralized SIEM forwarding retains the ProcessGuid-linked triad of Sysmon EID 1, EID 10, and EID 11. Permanently closing this attack surface requires enabling HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL = 1 (PsProtectedSignerLsa-Light, which rejects non-PPL OpenProcess calls at PsTestProtectedProcessIncompatibility) alongside VBS Credential Guard (isolating NTLM/TGT secrets inside VTL1 LsaIso.exe) and Defender ASR LSASS blocking.
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, Step #4 links Node ⑤ (C:\Windows\Temp\debug.dmp) and Node ⑥ (Sysmon EID 10 & PPL Watch) back to Node ④ (lsass.exe PID 684) to enforce RunAsPPL kernel protection and trigger SOC credential rotation.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Correlate SIEM alerts across Sysmon Event ID 1 (rundll32 + comsvcs/#24), Sysmon Event ID 10 (0x1010 + dbgcore.dll CallTrace), and Sysmon Event ID 11 (MDMP file creation), verify EDR ASR LSASS block logs, and audit HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL = 1 plus Credential Guard status across all Windows endpoints.
